material.name: high entropy superalloy (HESA)
material.initial_state: high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates

intervention.action: high temperature tensile testing and creep testing
intervention.description: Evaluation of tensile and creep behaviors

evidence_units.mechanism: Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate
evidence_spans: Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior.

material.name: high entropy superalloy (HESA)
material.initial_state: high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates

intervention.description: Evaluation of yield strengths

structure.description: high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates

evidence_units.mechanism: strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure
evidence_spans: The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures

Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure.

material.name: high entropy superalloy (HESA)
material.initial_state: high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates

intervention.description: Evaluation of creep resistance

structure.description: high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates

evidence_units.mechanism: strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure
evidence_spans: furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys.

material.name: HESA
material.initial_state: as-cast with dendritic microstructure and carbides

intervention.description: Heat treatment to form precipitates

structure.description: γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates

evidence_units.mechanism: Precipitation of γ′ phase creates a two-phase microstructure that contributes to high yield strength
evidence_spans: After the solution and aging heat-treatments, the microstructure consists of γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates is shown in Fig. 2(a) .
The γ′ precipitates appears to be spherical with an average size of 290 nm and 69 vol% measured by image analysis.
The precipitation strengthening has allowed HESA to possess higher tensile yield strengths than those of CoCrFeMnNi throughout the temperatures.

intervention.description: Calculation of anti-phase boundary (APB) energy

structure.description: γ′ phase with high Ti content

evidence_units.mechanism: High Ti content in γ′ phase significantly increases the anti-phase boundary (APB) energy
evidence_spans: According to JMatPro calculations, the APB energies of γ′ phase in HESA and CMSX-2 are 0.22 and 0.19 J/m 2 , respectively.
Consequently, higher APB energy of γ′ may contribute to some degree of strengthening in HESA [28] .

intervention.description: Measurement of tensile yield strength at various temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening and microstructural stability contribute to high yield strength
evidence_spans: The tensile yield strength versus temperature plot of HESA comparing to those of the commercial Ni-based superalloys [29] – [31] and reported high entropy alloys [10] , [32] – [34] are shown in Fig. 4 .
The precipitation strengthening has allowed HESA to possess higher tensile yield strengths than those of CoCrFeMnNi throughout the temperatures.
Furthermore, the tensile yield strengths of HESA are the highest among reported high entropy alloys.
Although the strengths of HESA are lower than those of CMSX-4 and CMSX-10, its behavior above 800 °C can be close to those of CMSX-2.

intervention.description: Creep behavior evaluation at high temperatures

evidence_units.mechanism: Positive lattice misfit drives rafting of γ′ precipitates along the stress axis

outcome.measurement_method: linear slope of ln ε ˙ vs. T −1

evidence_spans: Creep behaviors of HESA at 982, 850 and 750 °C under 159 MPa are shown in Fig. 5a,b,c .
From the linear slope of ln ε ˙ vs. T −1 curve, the creep activation energy of HESA can be estimated to be 290 kJ/mol, while that of CMSX-2 is 230 kJ/mol [37] .
Therefore, the rafting of γ′ in HESA has shown to coarsen along the direction of the applied stress, which can be related to the positive lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ′ [39] .

intervention.description: Observation of precipitate coarsening and dislocation behavior

structure.description: plate-like γ′ morphology with dislocation pile-up

evidence_units.mechanism: No shearing of γ′ phase by dislocations and rafting along stress axis
evidence_spans: The plate-like γ′ morphology of the 982 °C crept HESA is shown in Fig. 8(a) .
The average diameter of γ′ perpendicular to the stress axis has coarsened from 0.29 μm to 0.5 μm, while the average length in parallel direction extended to 3 μm.
Figure 8(b) shows the TEM analysis of crept HESA at 982 °C; dislocations have mainly piled-up within the γ matrix with no shearing the γ′ phase.

intervention.description: Creep tests at 750 and 850 °C for 800 h

evidence_units.mechanism: Stable spherical γ′ morphology resists creep deformation
evidence_spans: Figure 9a,b show the microstructures of HESA after 800 h interrupted creep at 750 and 850 °C.
The microstructure can be stable with high entropy γ matrix and L1 2 γ′, while the size of γ′ has increased from 0.3 μm to 0.4 and 0.6 μm after 750 and 850 °C creep tests, respectively.
Moreover, the morphology of γ′ has remained spherical, indicating that no rafting of γ′ has occurred in both conditions.
These stable γ′ morphologies can be beneficial to resist creep deformation

intervention.description: Observation of fracture surface morphology

structure.description: rough fracture surface with dimple and facet features

evidence_units.mechanism: Ductile necking dominates, with minor brittle fracture associated with carbides
evidence_spans: Figure 7(a) shows the side view of the 982 °C crept rupture specimen of HESA.
The diameter of the fractured gauge region has decreased from the original 6.35 mm to 4.75 mm, which demonstrates a ductile necking behavior before fracture.

According to Fig. 7(b) , the fracture surface is rough and with the majority dimple feature corresponding to ductile behaviour; however, minor brittle fracture regions reflected by facet-like morphology can be observed associated with the presence of carbides, Fig. 7(c) .

intervention.action: theoretical estimation based on strong-pair and weak-pair coupling theories
intervention.description: Estimating the optimized γ' size for peak strength and the resulting yield strength increment

structure.description: Precipitation strengthened structure with γ' precipitates

evidence_units.mechanism: The critical resolved shear stress (τc) is proportional to the square root of the γ' radius (r1/2) according to strong-pair and weak-pair coupling theories; increasing γ' size from the as-heat-treated 290 nm to the estimated optimized 390 nm would increase strength.
evidence_spans: Since these theories have indicated that the peak strength would be yielded as the r increases to around 2 T γ A P B [9] , and with the similar volume fraction of γ′ between HESA (69 vol%) and CMSX-2 (68 vol%), the optimized size of γ′ for peak strength in HESA can be estimated from that of CMSX-2.

As the τ c is proportional to r 1/2 , the strength of HESA may increase by 16% when its γ′ size increases from 290 to 390 nm, which would contribute to the room temperature tensile yield strength increment from 840 MPa to 960 MPa.
limitations: The optimized size of γ' (390 nm) was not achieved in the current work.

intervention.action: comparison of temperature dependence of yield strength
intervention.description: Analyzing the magnitude of positive temperature dependence on yield strength

structure.description: Precipitation strengthened structure with coherent precipitates

evidence_units.mechanism: The magnitude of positive temperature dependence on yield strength is influenced by the constrained lattice misfit (δ); a higher degree of |δ| leads to higher increase in yield strength due to stress fields around precipitates interacting with dislocations.

outcome.property: increase in tensile yield strength from room temperature to peak strength (Δσy)

evidence_spans: Furthermore, by comparing the increase in tensile yield strength from room temperature to the peak strength (Δσ y ) of CMSX-2 (960 to 1150 MPa) and HESA (840 to 855 MPa), the magnitude of positive temperature dependence on yield strength of HESA appears to be less pronounced.
Since the δ of CMSX-2 was reported around −0.33% [45] , its higher degree of misfit value would contribute to the higher strength.

intervention.description: Observing creep deformation behavior and microstructural changes

evidence_units.mechanism: Tertiary creep dominates the creep response of P-rafted superalloys due to the dominance of parallel rafting without perpendicular γ/γ′ interfaces, which differs from the N-rafting behavior that forms equilibrium interfacial dislocation networks to hinder dislocation movements.
evidence_spans: By contrast, the creep of HESA is dominated by parallel raft (P-raft) and without perpendicular γ/γ′ interfaces.
Tetzlaff et al . have reported that tertiary creep may dominate the creep response of P-rafted superalloys [47] , and this is exactly the creep behavior observed for HESA at 982 °C.
Therefore, higher creep rate of HESA compared to that of CMSX-2 could be a result of P-raft.
limitations: The specific quantitative creep strain rate values are not provided in this text segment.

intervention.action: theoretical analysis of deformation mechanism at intermediate temperatures
intervention.description: Identifying dislocation bypassing mechanism and factors influencing creep rate

structure.description: Un-rafted γ′ microstructure with γ matrix
defects: dislocations moving by climb and glide

evidence_units.mechanism: At low applied stress, thermally activated by-passing of dislocations around γ′ precipitates occurs, with inelastic deformation concentrating in the γ regions; sluggish diffusion of the higher entropy γ matrix, un-rafted γ′ microstructure, lower stacking fault energy (SFE), and higher activation energy of creep contribute to lower creep rates.
evidence_spans: On the other hand, HESA can exhibit the more comparable creep resistances to those of CMSX-2 at intermediate temperatures.
According to the creep behaviors of HESA shown in Fig. 5 , no obvious primary creep is observed, demonstrating that the dislocation shearing γ′ mechanism should not be applicable.

Instead, thermally activated by-passing of dislocations around γ′ precipitates should be the deformation mechanism with such low applied stress; [49] , [50] the inelastic deformation can essentially concentrate within the γ regions, where dislocations move by climb and glide processes to pass by γ′ particles [51] – [53] .
Therefore, the possible sluggish diffusion of the higher entropy γ matrix and the un-rafted γ′ microstructure can contribute to lower creep rate.
Furthermore, the lower stacking fault energy (SFE) of the γ matrix and higher activation energy of creep in HESA system would also be important strengthening factors.

The correlation between SFE, creep activation energy and creep strain rate is described as: ε ˙ = A ′ ( γ S F / G b ) 3 ( σ / G ) 5 exp ( − Q / R T ) , where A′ is a constant, γ SF is the stacking fault energy, G is the shear modulus, b is the Burgers vector, Q is the activation energy of creep and σ is the applied stress [29] , so the lower SFE and higher Q of HESA can lead to lower creep rates.
For materials possessing lower SFE, partial dislocations are more energetically favorable, and the spacing between partial dislocations can be increased.
As a result, the dislocations bowing around γ′ particles would become more difficult, which effectively decreases the creep strain rate.

material.name: HESA
material.composition: Rich in Ni, Co, Fe; contains Al, Ti, Nb, Cr, C, Mo, W
material.form: Ingot, plate form (1 cm x 1 cm x 3 mm), rod (6.35 mm diameter, 25.4 mm gauge length), flat tensile specimen
material.initial_state: Vacuum-arc-melted, directionally solidified (columnar microstructure), solution-heat-treated (1210 °C for 10 h)

intervention.description: Thermogravimetric analysis (TG/DTA) to determine solvus temperature

evidence_units.mechanism: Phase transformation detected by thermal analysis
evidence_spans: A Pyris Diamond TG/DTA was used to determine the γ′ solvus temperature of HESA; 30 mg sample was put in an Al 2 O 3 crucible with a heating rate of 10 °C/min to 1350 °C and with 400 sccm of Ar flow.

material.name: HESA
material.composition: Rich in Ni, Co, Fe; contains Al, Ti, Nb, Cr, C, Mo, W
material.form: Plate form (1 cm x 1 cm x 3 mm)

intervention.description: Characterization of γ/γ′ peaks using a heating stage

evidence_units.mechanism: Lattice parameter measurement via peak position deconvolution
evidence_spans: An X-ray diffractometer (Shimazu XRD-6000) with a heating stage and Cu-target radiation at 30 kV/20 mA was used to obtain the characteristic γ/γ′ peaks under a vacuum environment (1 × 10 −4 atm). The XRD specimens were in a plate form with dimension of 1 cm х 1 cm х 3 mm, and scanned at 2θ angle from 20 to 100° by 2 degree/min at room temperature and 982 °C. MDI Jade software was used to deconvolute the {200} lattice reflection and determine the peak positions of γ and γ′ for calculating the lattice misfit (δ).

material.name: HESA
material.composition: Rich in Ni, Co, Fe; contains Al, Ti, Nb, Cr, C, Mo, W

intervention.description: Annealing after indentation to induce cellular growth of γ′

structure.description: Coarsened γ/γ′ morphology due to cellular growth of γ′

evidence_units.mechanism: Strain aging induces coarsening of γ/γ′ morphology

outcome.property: Composition of γ and γ′ phases
outcome.measurement_method: EDS verification with lever rule analyses

evidence_spans: A strain aging method was conducted to assist measuring the compositions of γ and γ′ phase; samples were subjected to indentation after the solution-heat-treatment process stated above, and then followed by an annealing at 900 °C for 50 h. Therefore, cellular growth of γ′ would occur [20] , and resulted in the coarsened γ/γ′ morphology. In addition, the measured compositions of γ and γ′ were verified with the lever rule analyses.

material.name: HESA
material.composition: Rich in Ni, Co, Fe; contains Al, Ti, Nb, Cr, C, Mo, W

intervention.description: Mechanical testing under varying temperatures

evidence_spans: Tensile tests were conducted by a MTS 810 testing machine; flat tensile specimens were prepared by electrical discharge machining. The total length of a specimen is 43 mm, while the gauge length, width, and thickness are 19 mm, 10 mm, and 1.5 mm, respectively. The specimens were tensile tested at a stain rate of 10 −3 sec −1 from room temperature to 950 °C.

material.name: HESA
material.composition: Rich in Ni, Co, Fe; contains Al, Ti, Nb, Cr, C, Mo, W

intervention.description: Constant stress creep tests at elevated temperatures

outcome.measurement_method: ATS Series 2330 lever arm creep tester

evidence_spans: Creep tests were performed at 750, 850 and 982 °C with a constant stress of 159 MPa using an ATS Series 2330 lever arm creep tester. The dimension of rod specimens was machined to a diameter of 6.35 mm with a gage length of 25.4 mm according to the Japanese Industrial Standard (JIS-Z-2271 [56] ).
